tagline.text: A turquoise, tiered waterfall hidden in the forests of Burgos, Ilocos Norte

children.text: Tanap-Avis Falls is a basin-shaped waterfall inside the watershed forest of Barangay Tanap in Burgos, Ilocos Norte. A 20–40 minute forest walk from the village leads to turquoise pools and the falls, making it an easy half-day stop on a Pagudpud trip.

Tanap-Avis Falls lies in Barangay Tanap in the town of Burgos, in the northwest of Ilocos Norte. English Wikipedia describes it as a "basin-like waterfall," and its clear, turquoise-tinted water flowing down through rock pools is the main feature. The site is part of a watershed forest reserve under the National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS), a forest managed by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). So instead of a flashy resort, its biggest charm is that you reach it on foot through a rural landscape of small streams, forest, and rice fields.

For a long time the falls were visited mostly by locals and travelers who heard about them by word of mouth. According to a Philippine news report from March 2023, the Ilocos Norte provincial government spent

to build an eco-trail with walk boards, a view deck, and clean comfort rooms. In the same report, the governor said the upper stream still had to be fixed to bring more water to the falls. That suggests the water volume can vary a great deal with the season and the weather, so keep it in mind when you choose when to visit.
The falls are about
53km
north of Laoag, roughly
1 hour

by car, and fairly close to Pagudpud town along the coastal road. They combine well in one day with northern coast attractions such as the Bangui Windmills and Kapurpurawan Rock Formation. Burgos has another waterfall, Kaangrian Falls, but according to reviews the trail to Tanap-Avis is easier and it gets more visitors. The difficulty suits families with children and anyone who wants light trekking.

In short, Tanap-Avis Falls is not a big tourist attraction but a place for a "quiet forest walk and a swim." The low entrance fee and the local guides and tricycle drivers who lead the way keep costs small. On the other hand, there are clear things to watch out for, such as strong currents when the water is high, slippery rocks, and muddy trails in the rainy season. This guide covers how to get there, what each season looks like, costs, and safety rules, based on reviews and official information. Fees and operating details change often, so check the latest announcements. If you are going for the first time, set realistic expectations. This is not a giant waterfall but a small one reached by walking up a forest stream and resting in turquoise pools. According to reviews, the main drop is roughly

, so enjoy the atmosphere rather than the scale. It works best when combined with other sights in town for a full day. Northern Ilocos has strong midday sun, so bring a hat, sunscreen, and a change of clothes.

Water fills round pools between the rocks one after another as it flows down. When sunlight comes through the trees, the water shows a vivid turquoise, and the best time for photos is late morning to around noon.

A 2023 improvement project added walk boards, a view deck, and comfort rooms. Check the current condition locally, but some sections are easier to walk than before, which helps if you travel with children.
From the jump-off point to the falls you pass rice fields, small streams, and forest. Depending on the review it takes about
20–40 minutes
, and the last stretch may require pulling yourself up by tree roots and vines.

The pools at the edges are relatively shallow and good for soaking your feet and resting. However, right in front of the falls the water is deep with a current, so swim only in safe spots and use a life vest.
Many tricycle drivers in Burgos town are also registered guides. The official fee list has no guide fee, and a 2017 review put it at around
, but the current amount may differ, so confirm locally. Besides showing the way, they can tell you stories about the village.

blocks.title: A half-day combo with northern coast sights

children.text: Burgos has plenty to see, including a wind farm, a lighthouse, and coastal cliffs. Visit the falls in the morning, then tour Kapurpurawan Rock Formation or the Bangui Windmills in the afternoon for a natural full-day plan. The Bangui Windmills and Kapurpurawan Rock Formation both lie toward Burgos and Pagudpud, so the travel distances are short.

This is a watershed forest reserve, so the forest is relatively well preserved. You can enjoy a quiet atmosphere with only insects and running water to hear, and you must take all your trash with you.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: From Burgos town to the falls

children.text: Leave Laoag or Pagudpud and arrive in Burgos town (the plaza). Find a tricycle driver who also works as a guide here.
Ride the tricycle to the jump-off point in Barangay Tanap. At the registration desk at the entrance, pay an entrance fee of around
and sign in (confirm the fee locally).
Cross the stream at the jump-off point and enter the forest trail. Your shoes may get wet, so sandals or water shoes that can get wet are most comfortable.
Arrive at the falls. Take photos at the edge of the pools, and rest or dip your feet in a safe spot.
Head back the way you came. After rain the rocks are slippery, so go down slowly.
Return to town for lunch and move on to your next stop.
Times are examples. The falls are said to be open from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., but check the latest announcements.

items.title: Full-day course
items.subtitle: The falls and northern coast sights

children.text: Have breakfast in Pagudpud and set out for Burgos.
Trek to Tanap-Avis Falls.
Have lunch in Burgos town.
Visit coastal sights such as Kapurpurawan Rock Formation and the Bangui Windmills.
Return to Pagudpud or Laoag.
A tour that also includes Kaangrian Falls takes longer, so discuss the timing with your guide in advance.
You can fly from Manila (NAIA) to Laoag International Airport (LAO). Whether flights operate, and their times and durations, vary by season, so check airline announcements.
From the airport, go to Laoag city by taxi or tricycle.
Airfares and the number of flights vary a lot by season.
Long-distance buses run from Manila toward Laoag and Claveria, and according to reviews you can also take a Claveria-bound bus and ask to be dropped off in Burgos town.
The trip can be long, around 10 hours. Check departure times and fares with the bus company.
A bus from Laoag bus terminal toward Pagudpud or Burgos takes about
1–1.5 hours
. According to reviews the bus fare is around
The distance from Laoag to Burgos town is around
50km
From Burgos plaza to the jump-off point in Barangay Tanap, take a tricycle. According to reviews it costs around
per tricycle, carrying up to three people.
The road in Barangay Tanap is partly paved and partly unpaved. It may get worse when it rains, so ask the driver in advance.
You can also hire a tricycle directly from Pagudpud, but negotiate the fare beforehand and check road conditions locally.
The dry season from October to May is best for easy walking and clear water. According to one guide, from June to September the current gets stronger and the trail becomes slippery.

If you want to see the highest water volume you could aim for the end of the rainy season, but the risk of flash currents is high right after a typhoon, so avoid that time. Also ask locally before you go whether the provincial government has done work to increase the water volume.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, so most visitors stay in Pagudpud or Laoag. Pagudpud has many beach resorts and guesthouses and offers wide choice, while Laoag has good transport and is convenient for restaurants and facilities in the city. Room rates rise sharply in peak season, so book in advance.

It is best to eat in Burgos town. There are hardly any large restaurants at the falls entrance, so have lunch in town or bring water and snacks. Pinakbet, the signature Ilocano vegetable dish, and local seafood dishes can be enjoyed at restaurants in town or in Pagudpud.
If you leave early in the morning, you can see the falls quietly before the midday heat and crowds.
Wear water shoes or sandals that do not get slippery when wet, and avoid going barefoot because some rocks are sharp.
A guide is optional, but the cost is low and it helps the community, so we recommend one.
Bring cash in small bills. The entrance fee, guide, and tricycle are often all paid in cash.
Bring drinking water, snacks, a change of clothes, and a plastic bag, and take all your trash with you.
Check whether it rained the day before, and if it rained heavily, postpone the plan or stay away from the water.
If you combine it with Kaangrian Falls, allow plenty of time for the day and agree on the price with the guide in advance.
Some sections may have weak phone signal, so save an offline map.
After rain or right after a typhoon, flash currents can form, so avoid entering the water near the falls and cliff jumping.
Right in front of the falls the water is deep with a current, so people who are not strong swimmers should wear a life vest.
Do not copy locals who jump from the cliff. A bad landing can leave you caught in the current.
On rainy days and in the rainy season the rocks and dirt trail are slippery and muddy, so the risk of falling is high.
Entrance fees, operating hours, and trail conditions change often, so check the latest announcements locally or with a tourism office before you leave.
This is a protected area, so do not pick plants, make noise, or dump trash.
A white rock formation carved from coastal limestone by wind and waves, easy to combine on the same northern coast route.
Giant wind turbines lined up along the coast, the signature photo spot of northern Ilocos.
The northern tourism hub where beaches and resorts gather, with many choices for lodging and meals.
